title: Australia | ASIC Consumer Protection: Responsible Lending, DDO and Dispute Resolution
tagline: Learn the ASIC conduct rules Australian bank staff apply every day: trained and competent representatives, responsible lending, DDO, complaints and hardship.
sectors: Contact centres, branches and complaints teams
Bank compliance, risk and learning functions
description:
This quest teaches the consumer protection rules that **ASIC**, Australia's conduct and licensing regulator, applies to banks. It covers the general obligations of AFS and credit licensees in the **Corporations Act 2001 (s 912A)** and the **National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009 (s 47)**, including the duty to keep every representative **adequately trained and competent**; **responsible lending** under NCCP Act Chapter 3 and **RG 209**; the **design and distribution obligations** and **RG 274**; **internal dispute resolution** under **RG 271**, **AFCA**, hardship notices under the National Credit Code; and customers experiencing vulnerability. The **Banking Code of Practice** is explained as an ASIC-approved industry code that binds subscribing banks through their customer contracts.

It is designed for bank staff who provide financial products or consumer credit, their supervisors and the complaints, product and compliance teams around them: the representatives that licensees must keep trained and competent.

You follow a fictional team at Coral Range Bank in Brisbane, Logan, Townsville and Melbourne, and study real ASIC cases.

This quest builds knowledge of the law and good practice; it does not replace your institution's own policies, procedures or advice from your compliance team.
audience: Branch, contact centre and digital staff who deal in deposit, payment, card and insurance products
Home loan, personal loan and credit card lenders and credit assessors
Complaints, hardship and customer advocacy teams
Product owners, distribution managers and sales leaders
Team leaders, compliance and learning staff who supervise and train representatives
outcomes: Explain the general obligations of AFS and credit licensees and the duty to keep representatives adequately trained and competent
Apply the responsible lending steps: inquiry, verification, unsuitability assessment and written assessment
Apply the design and distribution obligations as an issuer or distributor, including review triggers and significant dealings
Handle complaints under RG 271, escalate systemic issues and explain the role of AFCA
Respond to hardship notices and customers experiencing vulnerability, and describe the Banking Code's contractual status
Identify the evidence, roles and timeframes ASIC expects a bank to show

quest.name: The Fair Deal Mission
quest.premise: You have just joined the conduct and compliance team at Coral Range Bank in Brisbane. With compliance head Mei Lin Zhao, learning lead Sofia Petrakis, home lending manager Liam Fitzgerald, complaints lead Kirra Watson and product manager Farid Haddad, you must turn ASIC's consumer protection rules into everyday decisions at the lending desk, on the product gate and at the complaints line.

badge.name: Fair Deal Guardian
badge.description: Awarded for demonstrating working knowledge of ASIC's consumer protection rules for Australian banks: competence, responsible lending, DDO and dispute resolution.

sessions.title: Licensee obligations and trained, competent representatives
sessions.summary: Meet the two licences a bank works under, the general obligations in Corporations Act s 912A and NCCP Act s 47, and the duty to keep every representative adequately trained and competent.
objectives: Explain why a bank holds an AFS licence and an Australian credit licence and what ASIC expects of each
Describe the main general obligations in Corporations Act s 912A(1) and NCCP Act s 47(1)
Apply the duty to keep representatives adequately trained and competent (s 912A(1)(f) and s 47(1)(g))
Recognise how RG 146, RG 206 and RG 105 shape initial and ongoing training
Explain when a licensee must report a reportable situation to ASIC

cards.title: Stage one: the licence on the wall
cards.setting: Conduct and Compliance floor, Coral Range Bank head office, Queen Street, Brisbane. 8:45 am.

lines.text: Your first morning at Coral Range Bank. In the lift lobby, two framed certificates hang side by side: an Australian financial services licence and an Australian credit licence.
Welcome aboard! I'm Mei Lin Zhao, head of conduct and compliance. Those two certificates are the reason this floor exists.
Sofia Petrakis, learning and competence lead. I look after who is allowed to talk to customers about which products, and how we prove they're ready.
Liam Fitzgerald, home lending manager at Logan. My new starters ask me the same thing every week: what am I actually allowed to say to a customer?
Kirra Watson, customer advocate and complaints lead. And when someone gets it wrong, the customer ends up talking to me.
Farid Haddad, products and distribution, Melbourne. Every product I design lives or dies on how well your people sell it.
So here's your quest: five stages, one final exam. Start with the promise behind those licences. What does ASIC expect of a licensee, and of every person who speaks for us?

cards.title: Two licences, one conduct regulator

scenes.heading: ASIC watches conduct
scenes.narration: The Australian Securities and Investments Commission, ASIC, licenses and supervises how financial services and consumer credit are provided. APRA looks after a bank's safety and soundness; ASIC looks after how it treats customers.

scenes.heading: The AFS licence
scenes.narration: Under the Corporations Act 2001, a bank needs an Australian financial services licence to deal in or advise on financial products such as deposit accounts, payment products and insurance it arranges.

scenes.heading: The credit licence
scenes.narration: Under the National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009, the NCCP Act, a bank needs an Australian credit licence to provide consumer credit such as home loans, personal loans and credit cards.

scenes.heading: General obligations
scenes.narration: Both Acts attach a list of general obligations to the licence. They are ongoing duties, not a one-off test at the licensing stage.

scenes.heading: People are the licence
scenes.narration: Both lists include the same promise: the licensee must make sure its representatives are adequately trained and competent for the services they provide. That is why this quest exists.

cards.title: Section 912A(1) and section 47(1) side by side
cards.caption: The two lists are close cousins. Learn them together and you understand most of what ASIC expects of a bank as a licensee.

items.label: Laws and representatives
items.left: Comply with financial services laws; reasonable steps so representatives comply
items.right: Comply with credit legislation; reasonable steps so representatives comply

items.label: Competence
items.left: Maintain competence; representatives adequately trained and competent (s 912A(1)(f))
items.right: Maintain competence; representatives adequately trained and competent (s 47(1)(g))

items.label: Disputes
items.left: IDR meeting ASIC standards plus AFCA membership (retail clients)
items.right: IDR meeting ASIC standards plus AFCA membership

items.label: Systems
items.left: Adequate resources and risk management systems
items.right: Compliance arrangements with a written plan

cards.question: A personal loan officer explains a credit card's fees incorrectly because nobody ever trained her on the product. Which licence duty is most directly engaged?
options: The duty to hold adequate financial resources
The duty to lodge annual financial statements
The duty to appoint a responsible manager for deposits
The duty to keep representatives adequately trained and competent for the credit activities they perform
cards.explanation: NCCP Act s 47(1)(g) requires a credit licensee to ensure its representatives are adequately trained and competent to engage in the credit activities authorised by the licence. The other options are not the duty this failure engages.

cards.title: What 'adequately trained and competent' means in practice
cards.body:
Neither Act sets a course length or exam. ASIC's guidance fills in the picture:

- **RG 206** (credit): the licensee decides what initial and ongoing training each representative needs and builds it into recruitment and training systems.
- **RG 146** (financial product advice): sets training standards for advisers. Staff who advise only on **basic deposit products** and related non-cash payment products can meet the standard through a course their licensee has assessed.
- **RG 105** (organisational competence): the licensee itself must keep the competence to provide its services, separate from the duty to train representatives.

The test is practical: could this person do this task, for this product, for this customer, correctly today? Training without assessment, refreshers or supervision rarely proves that.

cards.title: Match the duty to where it lives
cards.prompt: Link each obligation to its source.

pairs.right: AFS licensee must keep representatives adequately trained (including CPD where it applies) and competent
Credit licensee must keep representatives adequately trained and competent for authorised credit activities
Credit licensee must have compliance arrangements and a written plan documenting them
ASIC guide on training standards for financial product advisers, including basic deposit products
ASIC guide expecting credit licensees to set initial and ongoing training for representatives
AFS licensee must report reportable situations to ASIC within 30 days

cards.title: A turn: the 'reject' button

lines.text: Before you meet a customer, look at this public case. A big bank's staff kept pressing the wrong button in a hardship system.
Wrong button? That sounds like an IT problem, not a training problem.
It was both. Hundreds of customers who asked for hardship help never got the response the law requires. The Federal Court penalised the bank.
Systems fail when people don't understand what the system is for. That is exactly why 'adequately trained and competent' covers the tools people use, not just the rules.
So my induction checklist should cover the screens my lenders use, not only the law?
Yes. And then you check they can actually use them correctly.

cards.title: The fast-tracked transfer
cards.situation: Liam's branch is short-staffed. A teller, Josh, has six years on deposits but has never sold credit cards. Liam's regional manager wants Josh taking credit card applications from Monday because a promotion starts. The card module in the training system takes two days and includes an assessment. Josh says he 'watched someone do it once'.

choices.text: Keep Josh on deposits until he completes the card module and assessment, and ask for a trained lender to cover applications in the meantime.
choices.outcome: Best choice. The bank must ensure representatives are trained and competent for the credit activities they perform before they perform them. Recording the completion and the assessment also lets the bank prove it.

choices.text: Let Josh start Monday but have him complete the module by Friday.
choices.outcome: Partly right. Training will happen, but for a week customers deal with someone not yet shown to be competent. If something goes wrong, the bank cannot show it met its duty at the time.

choices.text: Let Josh start because six years of banking experience is enough for a simple card.
choices.outcome: Poor choice. Experience with deposits does not show competence in credit cards, which carry responsible lending duties. The licence duty is product and activity specific.

choices.text: Let Josh take applications as long as a lender signs every application afterwards.
choices.outcome: Partly helpful, but a sign-off after the conversation does not fix what Josh told the customer. Supervision supports training; it does not replace it.

cards.title: The competence cycle a licensee runs
cards.caption: RG 206 expects training to be built into recruitment and supervision. The cycle repeats whenever a role, a product or the law changes.

items.label: Define the role
items.detail: Which products and activities, for which customers

items.label: Train before doing
items.detail: Induction on law, product, systems and conduct

items.label: Assess
items.detail: Show the person can do the task correctly

items.label: Supervise and monitor
items.detail: File reviews, call reviews, complaints data

items.label: Refresh and update
items.detail: Ongoing training when law, products or risks change

cards.title: Myth or fact: training duties

cards.front: Myth: a one-off induction is enough.
cards.back: Fact: ASIC expects initial and ongoing training. Competence has to be kept up as products, systems and laws change.

cards.front: Myth: only financial advisers need training.
cards.back: Fact: the duty covers every representative who provides the licensed services, including lenders and staff who deal in deposit or payment products.

cards.front: Myth: ASIC approves each bank's training course.
cards.back: Fact: the licensee decides what is adequate. For basic deposit products, RG 146 lets the licensee assess the course itself.

cards.front: Myth: training records are optional.
cards.back: Fact: without records, the licensee cannot show it met the duty. ASIC will ask for evidence, not intentions.

cards.front: Myth: APRA banks are outside the credit licence duties.
cards.back: Fact: they hold credit licences too. Only some s 47(1) items, such as the resources and risk management limb, do not apply to APRA-regulated bodies.

cards.question: Coral Range Bank discovers that a pricing error has overcharged hundreds of credit card customers. Under the Corporations Act breach reporting regime, what must the AFS licensee consider?
options: Only whether customers complained, since reports are triggered by complaints
Whether APRA has already noticed, because APRA reports replace every ASIC duty
Nothing until the error has been fully remediated
Whether it is a reportable situation, and if so report to ASIC within 30 days of first knowing there are reasonable grounds to believe it has arisen
cards.explanation: Corporations Act s 912DAA requires a report within 30 days after the licensee first knows, or is reckless about whether, there are reasonable grounds to believe a reportable situation has arisen. Complaints and remediation do not start or stop the clock.

cards.title: Real case: Westpac and consumer credit insurance (2022)
cards.body:
In April 2022 the Federal Court ordered **Westpac** to pay a **$1.5 million** penalty, as reported in ASIC media release 22-084MR.

- Between 2015 and 2017 Westpac issued consumer credit insurance with credit cards and Flexi Loans to **141 customers** who had not asked for it.
- It then charged premiums the customers were not liable to pay.
- Westpac admitted contravening the ASIC Act ban on asserting a right to payment for unsolicited services, and **failing to comply with financial services laws** (Corporations Act s 912A(1)(c)).

**Lesson:** general obligations are not abstract. A gap in sales process and staff practice became a breach of the licence duties themselves.

cards.title: Real case: NAB, AFSH and the hardship button (2025)
cards.body:
In August 2025 the Federal Court ordered **National Australia Bank** and its subsidiary **AFSH Nominees** to pay a combined **$15.5 million** penalty (ASIC 25-165MR).

- Between 2018 and 2023 they failed to respond within the legal timeframe to **345 hardship applications**.
- ASIC said the failures arose mostly from staff **incorrectly using a 'reject' button** in the internal hardship system, so customers heard nothing.
- The banks also had to publish an adverse publicity notice and contact affected customers.

**Lesson:** competence includes knowing how the bank's own systems carry out legal duties.

cards.title: Stage one take-aways
items: A bank providing financial products and consumer credit holds an AFS licence and an Australian credit licence, both supervised by ASIC.
Both licences carry general obligations, starting with providing services efficiently, honestly and fairly.
Corporations Act s 912A(1)(f) and NCCP Act s 47(1)(g) require representatives to be adequately trained and competent.
ASIC expects initial and ongoing training, assessment and supervision built into recruitment (RG 206, RG 146).
Reportable situations must be reported to ASIC within 30 days under s 912DAA.

cards.prompt: Think of a product or system you use with customers. If ASIC asked tomorrow, what evidence could your bank show that you were trained and competent to use it before your first customer?

quiz.question: Which regulator licenses and supervises how Australian banks provide financial services and consumer credit to customers?
options: ASIC
APRA
AUSTRAC
The Reserve Bank of Australia
quiz.explanation: ASIC is the conduct and licensing regulator for financial services and consumer credit. APRA is the prudential regulator, AUSTRAC handles AML/CTF and the RBA runs monetary policy.

quiz.question: A new lender at Coral Range Bank will arrange personal loans for consumers. Which provision requires the bank to ensure she is adequately trained and competent for that work?
options: Corporations Act s 912A(1)(h)
NCCP Act s 133(1)
Corporations Act s 994B
NCCP Act s 47(1)(g)
quiz.explanation: Section 47(1)(g) of the NCCP Act is the credit licensee's duty to keep representatives adequately trained and competent. Section 912A(1)(h) is risk management, s 133 is the ban on unsuitable credit contracts and s 994B concerns target market determinations.

quiz.question: What does Corporations Act s 912A(1)(f) add to the training duty for AFS licensees that the credit provision does not mention?
options: Training must be approved in advance by ASIC
Training must be delivered by an external provider
Training includes complying with the CPD provisions where they apply
Training must be repeated every calendar month
quiz.explanation: Section 912A(1)(f) refers to representatives being adequately trained, including by complying with the CPD provisions, and competent. The Act does not require ASIC approval, external providers or monthly repetition.

quiz.question: Josh, a teller with long deposit experience, is asked to start taking credit card applications tomorrow without the card training. What is the best response?
options: Let him start because deposit experience shows competence
Let him start if a colleague sits within earshot
Let him start and record the training as completed later
Complete the card training and assessment before he takes applications
quiz.explanation: The duty is specific to the activity: he must be trained and competent for credit card applications before doing them. Deposit experience, informal oversight or back-dated records do not meet it.

quiz.question: According to RG 146, how can staff who advise only on basic deposit products meet the training standards?
options: By passing a national exam set by ASIC each year
By holding a university degree in finance
By completing a course their licensee has assessed as meeting the standards
By working under supervision for twelve months
quiz.explanation: RG 146 allows advisers on basic deposit products and related non-cash payment products to meet the standards through a course assessed by their licensee. It does not require a national ASIC exam, a degree or a fixed supervision period.

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects ASIC's expectation in RG 206 about credit representatives' training?
options: The licensee decides suitable initial and ongoing training and builds it into recruitment and training
ASIC sets one national syllabus every credit representative must follow
Training is only needed when a representative is first appointed
Training is optional if representatives work under a manager
quiz.explanation: RG 206 says ASIC generally expects the licensee to determine appropriate initial and ongoing training and embed it in recruitment and training systems. There is no single national syllabus, and supervision does not replace training.

quiz.question: Which general obligation sits at the top of both s 912A(1) and s 47(1)?
options: Holding capital above the regulatory minimum
Publishing annual customer satisfaction scores
Offering every product to every customer who applies
Doing all things necessary to provide the services efficiently, honestly and fairly
quiz.explanation: Paragraph (a) of both lists requires the licensee to do all things necessary so its services are provided efficiently, honestly and fairly. Capital is an APRA matter, and the other options are not licence obligations.

quiz.question: A bank finds a systems error that may have overcharged many customers. When does the 30-day period for reporting a reportable situation to ASIC start?
options: When the licensee first knows, or is reckless about, reasonable grounds to believe it has arisen
When the first customer complains about the error
When remediation payments are completed
When the board next meets to approve the report
quiz.explanation: Under s 912DAA(3), the report is due within 30 days after the licensee first knows that, or is reckless as to whether, there are reasonable grounds to believe the reportable situation has arisen. Complaints, remediation or board timing do not set the clock.

quiz.question: In the 2025 NAB and AFSH hardship case, what did ASIC say caused most of the missed responses?
options: Staff incorrectly using a 'reject' button in the hardship system
A deliberate policy to refuse all hardship requests
Customers sending hardship requests to the wrong bank
An outsourced call centre that closed without notice
quiz.explanation: ASIC's release explained that, with limited exceptions, the failures came from NAB staff incorrectly using a 'reject' function, so customers received no communication. That makes it a lesson in system competence, not deliberate policy.

quiz.question: Under NCCP Act s 47(1), which limb does NOT apply to a licensee that is regulated by APRA, such as a bank?
options: Keeping representatives trained and competent
Having adequate resources and adequate risk management systems
Being a member of the AFCA scheme
Engaging in credit activities efficiently, honestly and fairly
quiz.explanation: Section 47(1)(l), covering adequate resources and risk management systems, applies unless the licensee is a body regulated by APRA. The training, AFCA membership and efficiently honestly and fairly duties apply to banks in full.

sessions.title: Responsible lending under the NCCP Act and RG 209
sessions.summary: Work through the responsible lending obligations for credit providers: reasonable inquiries, verification, the unsuitability assessment, the written assessment and the records that prove it, with ASIC's views in RG 209.
objectives: Explain the three steps a credit provider must complete before entering a credit contract or increasing a limit
Apply the tests that make a credit contract unsuitable under NCCP Act ss 131 and 133
Use benchmarks, verification and scalability as RG 209 describes
Handle a consumer's request for a written copy of the assessment within the legal timeframes
Keep records that show the inquiries, verification and assessment were done

cards.title: Stage two: the refinance in a hurry
cards.setting: Logan branch lending office, south of Brisbane. 2:10 pm.

lines.text: Welcome to the lending desk. Meet today's file: a couple refinancing their home loan and adding $60,000 for a car and a holiday.
The application shows two salaries, a credit card, a buy now pay later account and living expenses entered as exactly the same number the system's benchmark suggests.
The broker says they're in a rush. Their old lender is slow and they want an answer by Friday.
Rushing is fine. Skipping steps is not. Tell me what you know about their requirements and objectives.
Refinance and a car. And a holiday, I think.
'I think' is where responsible lending starts. Inquire, verify, assess, then decide. And write it down.

cards.title: The responsible lending sequence

scenes.heading: Inquire
scenes.narration: Before assessing, the credit provider must make reasonable inquiries about the consumer's requirements and objectives, and about their financial situation.

scenes.heading: Verify
scenes.narration: It must also take reasonable steps to verify the consumer's financial situation. Asking is not enough; you check what you are told.

scenes.heading: Assess
scenes.narration: Then it must assess whether the credit contract will be unsuitable for the consumer, covering the period in which the credit is provided. The assessment must be made within the 90 days before the credit day.

scenes.heading: Do not lend if unsuitable
scenes.narration: If the contract is unsuitable, the licensee must not enter it, or increase the limit. Each of these duties is a civil penalty provision.

scenes.heading: Show your work
scenes.narration: On request, the consumer must get a free written copy of the assessment, and good records let the lender prove every step later.

cards.title: Before a credit day: NCCP Act ss 128-133
cards.caption: The same steps apply to a new credit contract and to an increase in a credit limit, and to unconditional representations that a consumer is eligible.

items.label: Reasonable inquiries
items.detail: Requirements and objectives; financial situation (s 130(1)(a)-(b))

items.label: Reasonable verification
items.detail: Steps to verify the financial situation (s 130(1)(c))

items.label: Unsuitability assessment
items.detail: Specifies its period; made within 90 days before the credit day (ss 128-129)

items.label: Unsuitable? Assess as unsuitable
items.detail: Inability to repay, or only with substantial hardship; or objectives not met (s 131)

items.label: Decide
items.detail: Must not enter or increase the limit if unsuitable (s 133)

items.label: Written copy on request
items.detail: Free of charge, within the set timeframes (s 132)

cards.question: Which two questions decide whether a credit contract is unsuitable under the NCCP Act?
options: Is the consumer's credit score above the bank's cut-off, and is the loan profitable?
Has the consumer banked with us before, and do they own property?
Is the interest rate competitive, and has the broker signed the file?
Can the consumer meet the obligations without substantial hardship, and does it meet their requirements and objectives?
cards.explanation: Sections 131(2) and 133(2) make a contract unsuitable if the consumer is likely to be unable to comply with the obligations, or only with substantial hardship, or if it does not meet their requirements or objectives (plus any circumstances the regulations prescribe).

cards.title: Substantial hardship: two presumptions to remember
cards.body:
The Act gives lenders two firm rules when judging whether a consumer could repay only with **substantial hardship**:

- **Selling the home.** If the consumer could only meet the obligations by selling their principal place of residence, the law presumes substantial hardship unless the contrary is proved (ss 131(3) and 133(3)).
- **Credit cards.** For a credit card contract, the consumer is taken to be in substantial hardship if they could not repay an amount equal to the credit limit within the period ASIC determines (s 131(3AA)).

Also remember **requirements and objectives**. A loan can be affordable and still unsuitable if it does not do what the consumer needs, for example a product with features they did not want and will pay for.

cards.title: Inquiry or verification?
cards.prompt: Sort each step into the part of s 130 it mainly serves.

items.text: Asking why the customer wants to refinance
Checking payslips against the stated salary
Asking about expected changes, such as parental leave
Reviewing bank statements for undisclosed debts
Asking which loan features matter to the customer
Confirming existing debts through a credit report
Asking about regular living expenses
Checking that stated rent matches the lease and transactions

cards.title: A turn: the benchmark shortcut

lines.text: Their declared living expenses match the benchmark figure to the dollar. Can I just use the benchmark and move on?
RG 209 is clear on that. A benchmark tells you nothing about this particular couple. It cannot confirm what they told you.
So what is it for?
Testing plausibility. If their figure is far below a realistic benchmark, that's a reason to ask more. It's a cross-check, not a substitute for inquiry and verification.
Liam pulls the bank statements. Two monthly payments to a car finance company appear that nobody mentioned.

cards.title: The undisclosed car loan
cards.situation: The couple's statements show two monthly payments to a car finance company that are not in the application. With them included, repayments on the new loan would leave very little each month. The broker says the car loan 'is being paid off soon' and asks you to approve today so the couple can settle on Friday.

choices.text: Pause the decision, ask the couple about the payments, verify the balance and payoff date, and reassess unsuitability with the debt included.
choices.outcome: Best choice. New information about the financial situation must be inquired into and verified before the assessment. If the loan would cause substantial hardship, it must be assessed as unsuitable and not entered.

choices.text: Approve now and note the broker's comment in the file.
choices.outcome: Poor choice. A broker's assurance is not verification, and the lender stays responsible for its own assessment. Approving with a known gap risks an unsuitable contract.

choices.text: Approve a smaller extra amount without asking, to leave a buffer.
choices.outcome: Partly sensible, but guessing does not meet the duty to inquire and verify. The assessment must rest on the consumer's real situation.

choices.text: Decline immediately and tell the broker the couple are unsuitable for any loan.
choices.outcome: Too fast. The undisclosed debt calls for inquiry, not an automatic refusal. Once verified, the couple may still qualify for a suitable amount.

cards.title: How much inquiry is reasonable? Scalability in RG 209
cards.caption: RG 209 calls this scalability: what is reasonable depends on the consumer and the credit. Inquiries never drop to zero.

axes.x: Size and complexity of the credit
axes.y: Risk signs in the consumer's situation

items.label: Light but real checks
items.detail: Small, short, simple credit for a consumer whose situation is clear

items.label: Deeper checks on the product
items.detail: Complex product or features the consumer may not understand

items.label: Deeper checks on the person
items.detail: Signs of stretch, irregular income or a vulnerable consumer

items.label: Most thorough inquiry and verification
items.detail: Large or long-term credit plus complexity or signs of stretch

cards.title: Answering a request for the written assessment
cards.prompt: Put the steps in order for a customer who asks for a copy of the assessment eight months after settlement.
steps: Log the request and the date the bank received it
Confirm the credit day and that the request falls within the 7-year window
Note the deadline: 7 business days, because it is within 2 years of the credit day
Retrieve the assessment from the loan records
Send a written copy without charging any fee
Record when and how the copy was given

cards.title: RG 209 at a glance

cards.front: What are benchmarks such as HEM for?
cards.back: A cross-check of plausibility. RG 209 says they give no information about the individual consumer and do not verify what the consumer said.

cards.front: Who must assess suitability: lender or broker?
cards.back: Each licensee has its own obligations. A lender can use information from a broker but remains responsible for its own inquiries, verification and assessment.

cards.front: What is 'scalability'?
cards.back: The idea that the inquiries and verification that are reasonable depend on the consumer's circumstances and the credit product.

cards.front: Why keep records?
cards.back: RG 209 warns that without records of inquiries, verification and information relied on, it is hard to show you complied.

cards.front: Does the duty cover limit increases?
cards.back: Yes. The steps apply before increasing a credit limit, not only before a new contract.

cards.front: Can a lender charge for the written assessment?
cards.back: No. The NCCP Act prohibits asking for payment for a copy of the assessment.

cards.question: A customer asks for a copy of her credit assessment three years after her personal loan started. What timeframe applies?
options: 7 business days after the request is received
21 business days after the request is received
30 calendar days after the request is received
No copy is required after two years
cards.explanation: Section 132(2) gives 7 business days for requests made within 2 years of the credit day, and 21 business days for later requests within the 7-year period. The copy must be free.

cards.title: Real case: ASIC v Westpac, the responsible lending appeal (2019-2020)
cards.body:
ASIC sued **Westpac** in 2017, alleging that between 2011 and 2015 its automated home loan process did not properly assess whether borrowers could meet repayments, partly because it relied on a living-expense benchmark.

- In **August 2019** Justice Perram dismissed the case (ASIC 19-210MR).
- In **June 2020** the Full Federal Court dismissed ASIC's appeal by a **2-1 majority** (ASIC 20-149MR).
- ASIC said it brought the case to get judicial clarity on a cornerstone duty, and later said it would not appeal further and would review its guidance.

**Lesson:** the law leaves lenders room in *how* they assess, but the steps of inquiry, verification and assessment still have to be done, and RG 209 explains ASIC's view of doing them well.

cards.title: Make your file tell the story
cards.body:
A reviewer who picks up your file should see, without asking you:

- the customer's **requirements and objectives** in their own words
- the **income, expenses and debts** you were told, and **what you checked** them against
- any **benchmark** comparison and what you did when figures looked low
- your **unsuitability conclusion** and the period it covers

RG 209 points to application forms, fact finds and needs analyses as practical ways to record this.

cards.title: Stage two take-aways
items: Before entering a credit contract or increasing a limit, inquire, verify and assess within the 90 days before the credit day.
A contract is unsuitable if the consumer likely cannot repay or only with substantial hardship, or it does not meet their requirements and objectives.
Selling the home to repay is presumed to be substantial hardship; credit cards are tested against repaying the limit within ASIC's period.
Benchmarks test plausibility; they do not replace inquiry or verification (RG 209).
Give a free written copy of the assessment on request within the legal timeframes, and keep records that prove each step.

cards.prompt: Pick a loan or limit increase you have seen recently. Which step, inquiry, verification or assessment, would have been hardest to prove from the file alone, and what would you add next time?

quiz.question: Before entering a credit contract, what must a credit provider do about the consumer's financial situation under s 130?
options: Obtain a credit score above a fixed national minimum
Accept the consumer's declaration if it is signed
Make reasonable inquiries and take reasonable steps to verify it
Ask the broker to confirm it in writing
quiz.explanation: Section 130(1) requires reasonable inquiries about the financial situation and reasonable steps to verify it. There is no national score threshold, and a signed declaration or broker confirmation does not replace the lender's own verification.

quiz.question: Within what period before the credit day must the unsuitability assessment be made, unless regulations prescribe otherwise?
options: 30 days
7 business days
90 days
12 months
quiz.explanation: Section 128 requires the assessment and the inquiries and verification to be made within 90 days (or another prescribed period) before the credit day.

quiz.question: A customer could repay a proposed loan only by selling her home. How does the NCCP Act treat this?
options: It is acceptable because the home secures the loan
It is a matter for her to decide, not the lender
It is presumed she could comply only with substantial hardship
It only matters if she has dependants
quiz.explanation: Sections 131(3) and 133(3) presume substantial hardship if the consumer could only comply by selling their principal place of residence, unless the contrary is proved.

quiz.question: A loan is affordable, but it includes an offset feature and redraw fees the customer said she does not want and will pay extra for. What is the main responsible lending concern?
options: It may not meet her requirements and objectives, which can make it unsuitable
None, because affordability is the only test
It breaches the design and distribution obligations automatically
It must be reported to AFCA within 30 days
quiz.explanation: Unsuitability has two limbs: inability to comply without substantial hardship, and failure to meet requirements or objectives. An affordable product can still be unsuitable on the second limb.

quiz.question: Liam sees declared living expenses that exactly match a benchmark figure. What does RG 209 say about using the benchmark here?
options: It can test plausibility but is not a substitute for inquiry and verification
It verifies the expenses, so no further steps are needed
It must never be used by lenders in any way
It replaces the need to ask about expenses
quiz.explanation: RG 209 says benchmarks give no information about the individual consumer and do not verify what they said, but can be used as a plausibility check. Banning them or relying on them alone both misread the guide.

quiz.question: How does the credit card test of substantial hardship in s 131(3AA) work?
options: Could the consumer pay the minimum repayment each month?
Has the consumer had a credit card for at least a year?
Could the consumer repay an amount equal to the limit within the period ASIC determines?
Is the limit below the consumer's monthly income?
quiz.explanation: For credit card contracts, the consumer is taken to be in substantial hardship if they could not repay an amount equal to the credit limit within the period ASIC determines under s 160F. Minimum repayments are not the test.

quiz.question: A broker sends Coral Range Bank a complete application with verified payslips. What remains the bank's responsibility as lender?
options: Nothing, because the broker carries all responsible lending duties
Only checking the broker's licence number
Only checking the security property valuation
Its own inquiries, verification and unsuitability assessment, using the broker's material as appropriate
quiz.explanation: Lenders and brokers each have responsible lending duties. RG 209 says lenders may use information obtained by a broker, but the lender's own obligations remain.

quiz.question: A customer asks for the written assessment before her loan is entered. What must the lender do?
options: Give her a written copy before entering the contract, free of charge
Give it within 21 business days after settlement
Give it only if she pays an administration fee
Refer her to AFCA for a copy
quiz.explanation: Under s 132(1), a request made before the contract is entered must be met with a written copy before entry, and s 132(4) bans charging for it.

quiz.question: What did the Full Federal Court decide in ASIC's responsible lending appeal against Westpac in 2020?
options: It ordered Westpac to pay a record penalty
It dismissed ASIC's appeal by a 2-1 majority
It found every Westpac home loan unsuitable
It sent the case to the High Court for decision
quiz.explanation: ASIC's release 20-149MR reported that the Full Federal Court dismissed the appeal two to one. No penalty was ordered, and ASIC later said it would not seek to appeal further.

quiz.question: Which practice does RG 209 suggest best helps a lender demonstrate compliance with its responsible lending duties?
options: Destroying working notes once a loan settles
Recording only the final approval decision
Relying on staff memory if ASIC asks
Recording inquiries, verification and the information relied on, using fact finds or needs analyses
quiz.explanation: RG 209 warns that failing to keep records of inquiries, verification and information relied on makes it hard to show compliance, and points to application forms, fact finds and needs analyses.

sessions.title: Design and distribution obligations and sales practices
sessions.summary: Learn how the design and distribution obligations (RG 274) steer bank products to the right customers, what distributors and frontline staff must do, and how poor sales practices turn into regulatory breaches.
objectives: Explain what a target market determination (TMD) must contain and which bank products need one
Describe the reasonable steps duty for issuers and distributors and the 10-business-day deadlines
Recognise review triggers and significant dealings and escalate them
Explain how training, incentives and scripts support distribution consistent with the TMD
Identify sales practices that ASIC has treated as harmful

cards.title: Stage three: the card everyone wants
cards.setting: Product team video call, Coral Range Bank Melbourne office and Brisbane. 9:30 am.

lines.text: Good news: our new rewards credit card launch is a hit. Applications are up, and the branch teams love the sales bonus.
Less good news: complaints too. Students saying they were signed up while opening a savings account, and people over their heads with the annual fee.
The TMD says the card is for people with steady income who pay the balance in full most months.
Then we have two questions. Is our distribution consistent with that target market? And is something telling us the TMD itself needs review?
And a third: do the people selling it know who the card is for?
This stage is about the product gate: the rules that decide which customers a product should reach.

cards.title: DDO in five scenes

scenes.heading: Design for someone
scenes.narration: Since 5 October 2021, issuers of most retail financial products must make a target market determination, a TMD, describing the class of consumers the product is designed for.

scenes.heading: Set the guardrails
scenes.narration: The TMD also sets distribution conditions, review triggers, review periods and the information distributors must report back, including complaint numbers.

scenes.heading: Reasonable steps
scenes.narration: Both issuer and distributor must take reasonable steps that will, or are reasonably likely to, result in distribution consistent with the TMD.

scenes.heading: Listen for triggers
scenes.narration: If a review trigger occurs, the issuer must review the TMD within 10 business days, and stop distributing until it has.

scenes.heading: Report significant dealings
scenes.narration: A distributor that learns of a significant dealing outside the TMD tells the issuer within 10 business days; the issuer tells ASIC within the same limit.

cards.title: Issuer and distributor duties under DDO
cards.caption: A bank is usually both: issuer of its own cards, loans and deposits, and distributor through branches, apps and contact centres.

items.label: Make the TMD
items.left: Prepare it and make it public, free, before distribution
items.right: Do not distribute unless a TMD has been made (s 994D)

items.label: Reasonable steps
items.right: Distribution consistent with the latest TMD (s 994E(3))

items.label: Reviews
items.left: Review when a trigger occurs and periodically (s 994C)
items.right: Report information the TMD asks for, including complaints

items.label: Significant dealings
items.right: Notify the issuer within 10 business days (s 994F(6))

cards.question: Which of these bank products is covered by the design and distribution obligations according to RG 274?
options: A margin lending facility
A consumer credit card issued by the bank
A MySuper product
Fully paid ordinary shares in the bank
cards.explanation: RG 274 lists credit facilities such as credit cards and home loans as covered, along with basic banking products. Margin lending, MySuper products and most ordinary shares are among the listed exclusions.

cards.title: What a TMD must contain
cards.body:
RG 274 summarises the content rules in s 994B(5). A TMD must be in writing and:

- describe the **target market**, the class of consumers the product is designed for
- set any **distribution conditions** and restrictions
- set **review triggers**, events suggesting the TMD may no longer be appropriate
- say when the **first and later reviews** happen
- set **reporting periods** for complaint numbers, and other information distributors must report

It must also be **appropriate**: if distributed under its conditions, the consumer is likely to be in the target market, and for a consumer in the target market the product is likely to fit their objectives, financial situation and needs.

Personal advice is **excluded conduct**, so some DDO duties do not apply when a licensed adviser gives personal advice.

cards.title: Inside the TMD or a distribution duty?
cards.prompt: Sort each item: is it content the issuer puts in the TMD, or a duty the distributor carries out?

items.text: Description of the class of consumers the card suits
Review triggers such as a spike in early cancellations
Reporting complaint numbers to the issuer each period
Distribution conditions, such as no sales through a store counter
Telling the issuer about a significant dealing within 10 business days
Keeping records of distribution information
The dates of the first and later TMD reviews
Not distributing before a TMD has been made

cards.title: A turn: the cancellation spike

lines.text: Look at this. A third of new card applications from our store partnership get cancelled within weeks.
And complaints are coming in from people who say they didn't understand they were applying for credit.
Our TMD lists unusually high cancellations as a review trigger. Do we keep selling while we look into it?
That is exactly what got another card issuer into Federal Court. If a trigger has happened and the TMD hasn't been reviewed, distribution must stop until it is.
Then I'll pause the channel today and start the review.

cards.title: The savings account cross-sell
cards.situation: A branch customer service officer, Mia, has a monthly target for the rewards credit card. A 19-year-old student opens a savings account and mentions she works six hours a week. Mia's script says to 'offer the card to every new customer'. The TMD describes consumers with steady income who usually repay the balance in full.

choices.text: Do not offer the card; help with the savings account, and raise with her manager that the script conflicts with the TMD.
choices.outcome: Best choice. Offering the card to a consumer clearly outside the target market is not consistent with the TMD, and the script itself is a distribution problem the bank must fix.

choices.text: Offer the card but explain the annual fee clearly.
choices.outcome: Partly right on disclosure, but the issue is target market fit. Clear disclosure does not make distribution consistent with the TMD.

choices.text: Offer the card because the script says to offer it to everyone.
choices.outcome: Poor choice. A script that ignores the TMD undermines the bank's reasonable steps and invites mis-selling.

choices.text: Offer a lower limit on the same card to fit her income.
choices.outcome: Still outside the target market, and responsible lending checks would also be engaged. A lower limit does not fix the mismatch.

cards.title: From product idea to the right customer
cards.caption: DDO controls the funnel at product level. Responsible lending and advice duties still apply to each individual customer.

items.label: All consumers
items.detail: Everyone who might hear about the product

items.label: Target market
items.detail: The class of consumers in the TMD

items.label: Distribution conditions
items.detail: Channels, eligibility checks and scripts

items.label: Responsible lending or suitability checks
items.detail: Each individual customer's situation

items.label: Right product, right customer
items.detail: Monitored through complaints and data

cards.title: Match the warning sign to the right response
cards.prompt: Link each situation to what the bank should do.

pairs.right: Review the TMD within 10 business days and pause distribution until reviewed
Distributor tells the issuer within 10 business days
Notify ASIC as soon as practicable, within 10 business days

pairs.left: Sales bonus drives sales outside the target market
pairs.right: Fix the incentive and retrain staff

pairs.left: Staff unsure who a product suits
pairs.right: Train on product attributes and the target market

cards.title: Sales practice red flags

cards.front: Add-on insurance 'just in case'
cards.back: ASIC's review of consumer credit insurance found poor value and harmful sales. Never add a product the customer did not ask for and agree to.

cards.front: 'Offer it to everyone' scripts
cards.back: Scripts must reflect distribution conditions. Blanket offers ignore the target market.

cards.front: Bonuses tied only to volume
cards.back: RG 274 says ASIC considers how distributors manage incentives that could encourage harm or distribution outside the TMD.

cards.front: Pressure to apply today
cards.back: Urgency stops customers understanding what they are applying for and undermines suitability checks.

cards.front: Credit offered during an unrelated task
cards.back: Opening a savings account is not a reason to apply for credit. Treat it as a separate, informed decision.

cards.question: RG 274 says ASIC will consider whether a distributor has trained staff involved in distribution. What does it suggest that training include?
options: Only the product's price and fees
Only techniques for overcoming customer objections
Only the bank's internal sales targets
Key product attributes and the target market, as well as appropriate sales conduct
cards.explanation: RG 274 says distributors should consider training staff on key product attributes and the target market, in addition to appropriate sales conduct, and assess their skills.

cards.title: Real case: American Express and the David Jones cards (2024)
cards.body:
In July 2024 the Federal Court ordered **American Express Australia** to pay **$8 million** for breaching the DDO, in ASIC's first civil penalty case under the regime (ASIC 24-158MR).

- The cards were co-branded David Jones credit cards, mainly sold in David Jones stores.
- From **25 May to 5 July 2022**, Amex ought to have known that **high cancelled application rates** suggested the TMDs were no longer appropriate, yet kept issuing the cards without reviewing them.
- The Court noted that staff responsible for monitoring the TMDs **were not aware of their obligations**.

**Lesson:** DDO is live monitoring, and people must know what the data is telling them.

cards.title: Real case: Westpac's unsolicited credit insurance (2022)
cards.body:
ASIC's 2022 release on **Westpac** (22-084MR) shows the sales side of the same problem.

- Westpac issued consumer credit insurance to **141 customers** who had not asked for it, then charged premiums; the Court ordered a **$1.5 million** penalty.
- ASIC said its earlier review of credit insurance across **11 banks and lenders** found poor value products and harmful sales practices.
- ASIC reported securing about **$270 million** in remediation across the sector.

**Lesson:** add-on sales need the customer's genuine request and agreement. Product design and sales conduct must both serve the customer.

cards.title: Stage three take-aways
items: Since 5 October 2021, issuers must make a TMD for covered products, including credit cards, home loans and basic banking products.
Issuers and distributors must take reasonable steps so distribution is consistent with the TMD.
Review triggers mean the TMD must be reviewed within 10 business days, and distribution paused until it is.
Significant dealings outside the TMD go to the issuer, and from the issuer to ASIC, within 10 business days.
Training on product attributes and target markets, sensible scripts and safe incentives are part of reasonable steps.

cards.prompt: Think of a product you sell or support. Could you describe its target market in one sentence to a customer? If not, what would help you learn it?

quiz.question: From what date did the design and distribution obligations apply to issuers and distributors?
options: 1 July 2019
28 February 2025
1 January 2023
5 October 2021
quiz.explanation: RG 274 states that issuers and distributors had to comply from 5 October 2021.

quiz.question: What is a target market determination (TMD)?
options: A credit assessment of one customer's ability to repay
ASIC's approval of a product before sale
A written document describing the class of consumers a product is designed for and how it should be distributed
A customer's statement of their financial goals
quiz.explanation: A TMD is the issuer's written description of the target market, distribution conditions, review triggers and reporting requirements. It is not an individual assessment or an ASIC approval.

quiz.question: A review trigger in a credit card's TMD has occurred. What must the issuer do?
options: Notify AFCA within 30 days
Review the TMD within 10 business days and not keep distributing until it has
Keep distributing until the next scheduled annual review
Ask distributors to collect more complaints first
quiz.explanation: RG 274 summarises s 994C: review within 10 business days of knowing, or when it ought reasonably to know, of the trigger. The Amex case shows the risk of continuing to issue without the review.

quiz.question: A Coral Range branch, acting as distributor, finds a significant dealing in a product that is not consistent with the TMD. What must it do?
options: Notify ASIC directly within 30 days
Record it and wait for the next audit
Tell the customer to complain to AFCA
Notify the issuer as soon as practicable, within 10 business days
quiz.explanation: Under s 994F(6), distributors notify the issuer of significant dealings within 10 business days. The issuer then notifies ASIC under s 994G.

quiz.question: Which product is excluded from the design and distribution obligations according to RG 274?
options: A home loan for a consumer
A 31-day term deposit
A consumer credit card
A margin lending facility
quiz.explanation: RG 274 lists margin lending facilities among excluded products. Home loans and credit cards are covered credit facilities, and basic banking products, which include 31-day term deposits, are prescribed as needing a TMD.

quiz.question: Why do some DDO duties not apply when a licensed adviser gives a customer personal advice?
options: Advisers are exempt from all ASIC regulation
Personal advice only applies to superannuation
Personal advice is 'excluded conduct' under the DDO regime
ASIC approves each piece of personal advice in advance
quiz.explanation: RG 274 explains that personal advice is excluded conduct, so duties such as the reasonable steps obligation for distributors do not apply to it. Advisers remain subject to their own advice obligations.

quiz.question: In the 2024 American Express case, what signal should have prompted a TMD review?
options: A fall in the cash rate
High rates of cancelled credit card applications
A competitor launching a new card
A drop in the store's foot traffic
quiz.explanation: ASIC's release says the Court found Amex ought to have known that high cancelled application rates reasonably suggested the TMDs were no longer appropriate, yet kept issuing the cards.

quiz.question: A branch script tells staff to offer a rewards credit card to every new savings customer. Which DDO concern is most direct?
options: The script breaches the credit card interest rate cap
Distribution may not be consistent with the TMD, undermining the bank's reasonable steps
The script must first be lodged with AFCA
Savings accounts cannot be sold with any other product
quiz.explanation: Reasonable steps include distribution conditions, scripts and controls that keep sales within the target market. A blanket offer ignores the TMD. The other options describe rules that do not exist.

quiz.question: What does RG 274 say ASIC will take into account about distributors' staff incentives?
options: Steps taken to eliminate or manage the risk that incentives encourage harm or sales outside the TMD
Whether incentives are paid in cash or shares
Whether incentives exceed a fixed percentage of salary
Nothing, because incentives are an employment matter
quiz.explanation: RG 274 lists inappropriate incentives as a factor: ASIC considers how a distributor eliminates or manages the risk that incentives encourage consumer harm or inconsistent distribution.

quiz.question: Which records must a distributor keep under the DDO regime?
options: Only signed customer applications
Distribution information, including the number of complaints about the product
Only the issuer's TMD reviews
Only staff sales targets
quiz.explanation: RG 274 summarises s 994F(3): distributors must keep complete and accurate records of distribution information, including complaint numbers and information the TMD specifies.

sessions.title: Complaints, AFCA, hardship and customers experiencing vulnerability
sessions.summary: Handle complaints under RG 271 and send unresolved ones to AFCA, respond to hardship notices on time, support customers experiencing vulnerability, and understand where the Banking Code of Practice fits.
objectives: Recognise a complaint using the definition RG 271 adopts, in any channel
Apply the RG 271 response timeframes, the five-business-day rule and IDR delay notifications
Explain the role of AFCA and what an IDR response must tell the customer
Respond to a hardship notice in line with National Credit Code s 72
Support customers experiencing vulnerability and explain the Banking Code's contractual status

cards.title: Stage four: the comment on the bank's page
cards.setting: Complaints team, Coral Range Bank contact centre, Townsville. 10:05 am.

lines.text: Welcome to the listening post. Every complaint here is free advice about what we're getting wrong.

On screen: a post on the bank's own social media page. 'Third time I've rung about my loan. Nobody calls back. I lost my job and I can't keep paying. Disgraceful.' The author's name and profile are visible.
That's a social media rant, surely. Not a formal complaint. She hasn't even used the word.
Under RG 271 she doesn't need to. It's an expression of dissatisfaction on our own channel, she's identifiable and contactable, and she clearly expects a response.
And look again. 'I lost my job and I can't keep paying.' That may also be a hardship notice.
So two clocks may have just started. Let's learn to read them.

cards.title: How a complaint travels

scenes.heading: Recognise it
scenes.narration: RG 271 adopts the definition in the Australian standard AS/NZS 10002:2014: an expression of dissatisfaction where a response or resolution is explicitly or implicitly expected. It can be spoken, written or posted on the firm's own social media.

scenes.heading: Acknowledge it
scenes.narration: ASIC expects firms to acknowledge a complaint within 24 hours, or one business day, or as soon as practicable.

scenes.heading: Resolve it
scenes.narration: Most complaints need a written IDR response within 30 calendar days. Credit complaints about hardship notices or default notices have 21 days.

scenes.heading: Explain the outcome
scenes.narration: The IDR response gives the final outcome, reasons if the complaint is rejected, and the customer's right to go to AFCA with AFCA's contact details.

scenes.heading: AFCA if needed
scenes.narration: The Australian Financial Complaints Authority is the external dispute resolution scheme. Banks must be members, and customers can take complaints the bank has not resolved to AFCA.

cards.title: RG 271 maximum timeframes for an IDR response
cards.caption: Timeframes run in calendar days unless marked as business days. Day 1 is the first day after the complaint is received.

items.label: Acknowledge
items.detail: ASIC expects acknowledgement within 24 hours or one business day

items.label: Quick closure
items.detail: No IDR response needed if resolved to satisfaction or explained, unless an exception applies

items.label: Hardship and default notices
items.detail: Credit complaints involving hardship notices or default notices

items.label: Standard complaints
items.detail: Written IDR response, or an IDR delay notification with reasons

items.label: Super trustees
items.detail: Most superannuation trustee complaints

cards.question: A customer tells a teller, angrily, that a fee was charged twice. She doesn't use the word 'complaint' and doesn't put anything in writing. Under RG 271, what is this?
options: Feedback only, because it was verbal
A complaint that must go through the IDR process
An inquiry, because she did not say 'complaint'
Not a complaint until she writes to the bank
cards.explanation: RG 271 says consumers do not need to use the word 'complaint' or write it down. Firms must not class a complaint as feedback or an inquiry just because it was verbal.

cards.title: The five-business-day rule and its exceptions
cards.body:
A firm does not need to send a written IDR response if, by the end of the **fifth business day** after receipt, it has:

- resolved the complaint to the customer's satisfaction, or
- given an explanation or apology when it can take no further reasonable action.

But a **written IDR response is still required** if:

- the customer asks for one
- the complaint is about **hardship**, a **declined insurance claim** or the **value of a claim**
- it concerns certain superannuation trustee decisions

And whatever the timeframe, if the firm cannot respond in time, it must send an **IDR delay notification** that gives the real reasons for the delay and the right to go to AFCA. 'Our investigation is ongoing' is not a reason.

cards.title: Complaint or not?

items.text: A verbal grumble about a double fee charge, expecting a fix
A post on the bank's own page by a named, contactable customer, upset about delays
A question about branch opening hours
Dissatisfaction resolved with a goodwill payment and no admission of error
A complaint about delays in an existing remediation program
A request to update a home address
A complaint the bank thinks has no merit
A thank-you email praising a lender

cards.title: A turn: hardship hidden in a complaint

lines.text: Our customer, Mrs Talbot, confirms she lost her job last month. She wants to reduce her home loan repayments for a while.
Do we treat it as a complaint or a hardship request?
Both. The complaint is about nobody calling back. Her words about being unable to pay are a hardship notice, and it can be given orally.
Under the National Credit Code we must respond with our decision within the time the law sets. If we don't agree a change, the notice must give reasons and AFCA's details.
Large banks have paid heavy penalties for missing exactly this. We log it now, with today's date.

cards.title: The missing hardship request
cards.situation: Mrs Talbot says she used the online hardship form three weeks ago and heard nothing. You check: the form arrived, but was routed to an inbox nobody monitors. She is now behind on repayments and has received a collections call. She is upset and says she feels ashamed to be asking.

choices.text: Apologise, pause collections, log a complaint and a hardship request, escalate the unmonitored inbox as a possible systemic issue, and assess her hardship request quickly.
choices.outcome: Best choice. It treats her with care, protects her while the request is considered, meets IDR and hardship duties, and gets the system fault investigated so other customers are found too.

choices.text: Ask her to submit the form again so the clock restarts from today.
choices.outcome: Poor choice. The bank received her request three weeks ago. Asking her to resubmit hides the failure and may breach hardship timeframes.

choices.text: Assess her hardship request but leave the inbox issue for IT to find.
choices.outcome: Partly right. Her request is handled, but RG 271 requires firms to escalate possible systemic issues promptly. Other customers may be in the same inbox.

choices.text: Refer her straight to AFCA because the complaint is serious.
choices.outcome: Not the first step. The bank must deal with the complaint through IDR and respond to the hardship notice. AFCA is for complaints the bank does not resolve.

cards.title: From one complaint to fixing the system
cards.caption: RG 271 says boards must set clear accountabilities for complaints handling, including systemic issues.

items.label: Staff spot a pattern
items.detail: RG 271 requires firms to encourage staff to escalate possible systemic issues

items.label: Analyse complaint data
items.detail: Regular analysis to find issues affecting more than one customer

items.label: Escalate and investigate
items.detail: Promptly, to the right area of the bank

items.label: Remediate
items.detail: Identify affected customers and provide fair remediation

items.label: Report and learn
items.detail: Board reports include complaint metrics and systemic issues

cards.title: Banking Code of Practice: what it is and is not
cards.prompt: Match each statement to the right fact, based on ASIC's 2024 approval release.

pairs.right: The Australian Banking Association, which develops and reviews it
Its rules form part of subscribing banks' contracts with customers and guarantors
The Banking Code Compliance Committee, not ASIC
Approved by ASIC; took effect on 28 February 2025
Care and skill of a diligent and prudent banker for consumer borrowers and guarantors

cards.title: Customers experiencing vulnerability

cards.front: What can make a customer vulnerable?
cards.back: Life events such as job loss, serious illness, family violence or natural disaster, as well as disability, language barriers or age. Anyone can become vulnerable.

cards.front: Do customers have to say 'I am vulnerable'?
cards.back: No. Listen for cues, ask open questions, and offer help without forcing disclosure.

cards.front: What does RG 271 expect on accessibility?
cards.back: An IDR process easy to use, including for people with disability or language difficulties, and staff trained to identify and help people who need support to complain.

cards.front: What did the 2025 Banking Code broaden?
cards.back: ASIC's approval release says it broadened the meaning of financial difficulty and improved inclusion, including interpreter services.

cards.front: Why does it matter legally?
cards.back: Hardship failures have led to large penalties, and courts have stressed that affected customers were often in very vulnerable situations.

cards.question: Coral Range Bank refuses Mrs Talbot's hardship request. What must its notice under National Credit Code s 72(4) include?
options: That no change was agreed, the reasons, and AFCA's name, contact details and her rights under it
Only that no change was agreed
A referral to a debt collector
An offer to sell the property for her
cards.explanation: Section 72(4)(b) requires a notice stating that the parties have not agreed to change the contract, the reasons, AFCA's name and contact details, and the debtor's rights under the AFCA scheme.

cards.title: Real case: Westpac's missed hardship requests (2026)
cards.body:
In May 2026 the Federal Court ordered **Westpac** to pay **$26 million** (ASIC 26-107MR).

- Westpac and its brands St George, BankSA and Bank of Melbourne failed to respond in time to **over 200 online hardship requests** between 2017 and 2023.
- Justice McEvoy found the failures, though not deliberate, **grossly negligent**, and noted that some customers had adverse credit information recorded and debts sold.
- Westpac admitted contraventions of National Credit Code s 72(4) and the NCCP Act duty to act efficiently, honestly and fairly, and paid over **$1.7 million** in remediation.

ASIC's release also noted **ANZ** was ordered to pay **$40 million** for hardship failures (25-314MR).

cards.title: Real case: Telstra Super and IDR timeframes (2026)
cards.body:
In April 2026 the Federal Court found **Telstra Super** failed to comply with the enforceable IDR requirements, in **the first case ASIC brought under them** (ASIC 26-091MR).

- About **one third** of relevant complaints were not answered within the **45-day** superannuation timeframe; some took more than 100 days.
- Some members were not told the reasons for delay or their right to go to AFCA.
- The judge said a delay notice that merely says the investigation is 'ongoing' does **not** give a reason for the delay.

**Lesson for banks:** the same enforceable standards apply to bank complaints, with 30-day and 21-day timeframes.

cards.title: Stage four take-aways
items: A complaint is any expression of dissatisfaction expecting a response; it can be verbal or on the bank's own social media.
Standard complaints get a written IDR response within 30 calendar days; hardship and default notice complaints within 21.
IDR responses give the outcome, reasons for any rejection and the right to go to AFCA; delay notices need real reasons.
A hardship notice can be oral; the credit provider must respond as National Credit Code s 72 requires.
The Banking Code binds subscribing banks through their customer contracts; ASIC approves it but does not enforce it.

cards.prompt: Recall a time a customer expressed frustration to you without calling it a complaint. How would you handle it now, and what clue might have signalled hardship or vulnerability?

quiz.question: Which definition of 'complaint' does RG 271 require financial firms to adopt?
options: The definition in AS/NZS 10002:2014
The definition in the firm's own complaints policy
Any written complaint marked 'formal'
The definition in the Banking Code of Practice
quiz.explanation: RG 271 requires the IDR process to adopt the AS/NZS 10002:2014 definition: an expression of dissatisfaction where a response or resolution is explicitly or implicitly expected or legally required.

quiz.question: What is the maximum timeframe for an IDR response to a standard bank complaint under RG 271?
options: 45 calendar days after receiving the complaint
21 business days after receiving the complaint
10 business days after receiving the complaint
30 calendar days after receiving the complaint
quiz.explanation: RG 271 sets 30 calendar days for standard complaints. 45 days applies to most superannuation trustee complaints and 21 days to credit complaints involving hardship or default notices.

quiz.question: A customer complains about the bank's handling of her hardship request. The bank resolves it on day 3. Must it still send a written IDR response?
options: Yes, because hardship complaints need a written IDR response even if closed within five business days
No, because it was closed within five business days
Only if AFCA asks for one
Only if the customer pays a fee for it
quiz.explanation: RG 271.75 requires a written IDR response for complaints about hardship even when closed by the end of the fifth business day.

quiz.question: Which of these must an IDR response tell a complainant?
options: The names of every staff member involved
The bank's profit on the product
The final outcome, her right to take the complaint to AFCA and AFCA's contact details
How to complain to APRA instead
quiz.explanation: RG 271.53 lists the final outcome, the right to take the complaint to AFCA, and AFCA's contact details. Staff names, profit figures and APRA are not required.

quiz.question: The bank cannot finish investigating a complex complaint within 30 days. What must it send?
options: Nothing until the investigation finishes
A letter saying 'our investigation is ongoing'
A request that the customer withdraw the complaint
An IDR delay notification giving the reasons for the delay and the right to go to AFCA
quiz.explanation: RG 271 requires an IDR delay notification. In the Telstra Super case the Court held that saying an investigation is ongoing is not a reason for delay.

quiz.question: A named, contactable customer posts on Coral Range Bank's own social media page that her card was charged twice and she wants it fixed. How should staff treat it?
options: As public feedback that needs no response
As a complaint to be handled through IDR, with care to protect her privacy
As a complaint only if she also emails
As a matter for the social media agency
quiz.explanation: RG 271.32 treats posts on a firm's own social media by identifiable, contactable authors as complaints if they meet the definition. Firms must protect privacy when responding.

quiz.question: A borrower phones to say she has lost her job and cannot keep up repayments. Under National Credit Code s 72, what is this?
options: Not a hardship notice until she completes a form
A complaint that must go straight to AFCA
A hardship notice, which can be given orally
A default notice issued by the borrower
quiz.explanation: Section 72(1) allows a debtor to give a hardship notice orally or in writing. The bank must then respond in line with s 72, with the AFCA details if no change is agreed.

quiz.question: What did ASIC's 2024 release say about the Banking Code of Practice's legal effect?
options: It is a law passed by Parliament and enforced by ASIC
Its rules bind ABA members and form part of their contracts with customers; ASIC does not enforce it
It applies to every lender in Australia, whether or not it subscribes
It replaces the NCCP Act for subscribing banks
quiz.explanation: ASIC's 24-136MR says the Code's rules are binding on ABA members and form part of contracts with customers, ASIC has no role in enforcing or monitoring compliance, and the Banking Code Compliance Committee oversees it.

quiz.question: Under RG 271, what must a firm do when staff spot what may be a systemic issue from complaints?
options: Enable staff to escalate it and promptly escalate it for investigation and action
Wait until AFCA identifies it
Handle each complaint separately without escalation
Report it only in the annual report
quiz.explanation: RG 271.120 requires firms to encourage and enable staff to escalate possible systemic issues, analyse complaint data, escalate promptly and report internally on outcomes.

quiz.question: In the 2026 Westpac hardship case, how did Justice McEvoy characterise the contraventions?
options: Deliberate and dishonest
Not deliberate, but grossly negligent
Minor technical breaches
Caused entirely by customers' errors
quiz.explanation: ASIC's 26-107MR quotes the judge accepting that the contraventions were not suggested to be deliberate, arose from inadequate systems, and were grossly negligent.

sessions.title: Assessment readiness: the conduct framework, roles and evidence
sessions.summary: Pull the quest together: how a bank shows ASIC that its people are trained and competent, how complaints, lending files and product data feed each other, who does what, and when to report.
objectives: Describe the parts of a bank's conduct framework that ASIC would expect to see
Connect complaints data, DDO reviews, responsible lending files and breach reporting
Explain the roles of frontline staff, team leaders, product owners, complaints, compliance and the board
Identify the records that prove training, lending, distribution and complaint duties were met
Recall the key timeframes and obligations covered across the quest

cards.title: Stage five: the review is coming
cards.setting: Boardroom annex, Coral Range Bank head office, Brisbane. 4:00 pm.

lines.text: Final stage. Imagine ASIC writes tomorrow asking how we know our lenders, tellers and complaints staff are competent. What do we send?
Training records for every representative: what they completed, when, the assessment result, and refreshers.
Lending files that show inquiries, verification and the unsuitability assessment.
TMDs, review records and the data we watched, including complaint numbers from distributors.
Our complaints register, timeframes met, delay notices, and the systemic issues we escalated.
Good. Now prove they connect. ASIC looks for one system, not five separate filing cabinets.

cards.title: One conduct system, many duties

scenes.heading: Start with the licence duties
scenes.narration: Everything hangs off the general obligations: efficiently, honestly and fairly; comply with the law; take reasonable steps so representatives comply; keep them trained and competent.

scenes.heading: Train and assess
scenes.narration: Each role gets induction and ongoing training matched to its products and tasks, with an assessment that shows competence, and records that prove it.

scenes.heading: Connect the signals
scenes.narration: Complaints feed DDO reviews. Lending file reviews feed training. Systemic issues feed remediation. One signal should reach every team that needs it.

scenes.heading: Escalate and report
scenes.narration: Breaches and possible breaches are escalated quickly so the licensee can decide whether a reportable situation must go to ASIC within 30 days.

scenes.heading: Board oversight
scenes.narration: RG 271 says boards must set clear accountabilities for complaints and systemic issues, and board reports must include complaint metrics and analysis.

cards.title: Who owns what in the conduct framework
cards.caption: Each layer depends on the one below spotting issues early and the one above acting on them.

items.label: Board
items.detail: Sets accountabilities; receives complaint metrics and systemic issue analysis

items.label: Senior management
items.detail: Resources, incentives and culture; signs off TMDs and remediation

items.label: Compliance and risk
items.detail: Monitoring, testing, breach assessment and reporting to ASIC

items.label: Product owners and complaints team
items.detail: TMD reviews, complaint analysis, systemic issue escalation

items.label: Team leaders
items.detail: Supervision, file and call reviews, coaching

items.label: Frontline representatives
items.detail: Apply training with every customer; escalate concerns

cards.question: Which evidence best shows ASIC that a credit representative was adequately trained and competent before advising customers?
options: Her job title and years of service
A signed code of conduct
A note that she attended a team meeting
A dated record of completed role training and a passed assessment, before the first customer contact
cards.explanation: The duty is to ensure representatives are trained and competent for the activities they perform. A dated training and assessment record that predates customer contact is the clearest proof.

cards.title: The evidence map
cards.body:
When ASIC tests a bank's conduct, it typically asks for evidence like this:

| Duty | Typical evidence |
|---|---|
| Trained and competent (s 912A(1)(f), s 47(1)(g)) | Training plans by role, completion and assessment records, refresher logs |
