| Compliance arrangements (s 47(1)(k)) | The written compliance plan and monitoring results |
| Responsible lending | Fact finds, verification documents, assessments, file reviews |
| DDO | TMDs, review records and reasons, distributor reports, significant dealing notices |
| IDR | Complaints register, timeframes met, IDR responses, delay notices, systemic issue reports |
| Breach reporting | Breach register, assessments and reports lodged with ASIC |

If it isn't recorded, it is very hard to prove it happened.

cards.title: From a complaint to a reportable situation
cards.prompt: Put the steps in the order a well-run bank would follow.
steps: Frontline staff log a complaint about a fee charged twice
Complaints team spots many similar complaints and escalates a possible systemic issue
Investigation finds a systems error affecting thousands of accounts
Compliance assesses whether it is a reportable situation
The bank reports to ASIC within 30 days of reasonable grounds to believe it arose
Affected customers are identified and remediated, and staff guidance is updated

cards.title: A turn: the mock review

lines.text: I ran a mock review on ten home loan files. Eight are great. Two have no verification of living expenses, just the benchmark.
Both from the same new lender. She joined in a rush during the refinance boom.
And her training record shows the responsible lending module was booked but never completed.
So this is not just two bad files. It is a training and supervision gap, and possibly a breach to assess.
And if any of those customers complain, I need to know the context.

cards.title: Closing the gap
cards.situation: The new lender has written 14 home loans in six weeks without completing responsible lending training. Two of ten sampled files lack verification of living expenses. The regional manager suggests quietly completing her training and moving on, since 'no customer has complained yet'.

choices.text: Stop her from approving loans until trained and assessed, review all 14 files, remediate any unsuitable lending, and refer the matter to compliance for breach assessment.
choices.outcome: Best choice. It protects customers, fixes the competence gap, checks the full population of files and lets compliance decide if there is a reportable situation within the 30-day window.

choices.text: Complete her training this week and review only the two failed files.
choices.outcome: Partly right. Training fixes the future, but the other 12 files may have the same gap, and breach assessment is still needed.

choices.text: Do nothing until a customer complains.
choices.outcome: Poor choice. The duty to train is not triggered by complaints, and waiting risks harm, larger remediation and a late breach report.

choices.text: Move her to a deposits role and close the matter.
choices.outcome: Removes the immediate risk but leaves possible unsuitable loans and an unassessed breach. ASIC expects the problem itself to be fixed.

cards.title: Real cases from this quest
cards.caption: Common threads: systems people did not understand, signals nobody acted on, and customers who needed help and did not get it.

items.label: Westpac, 2026
items.detail: Penalty for failing to respond in time to over 200 online hardship requests (ASIC 26-107MR)

items.label: NAB and AFSH, 2025
items.detail: Penalty for 345 hardship applications not answered in time (ASIC 25-165MR)

items.label: American Express, 2024
items.detail: First DDO civil penalty: cards issued without reviewing TMDs after a trigger (ASIC 24-158MR)

items.label: Westpac, 2022
items.detail: Consumer credit insurance issued to 141 customers who had not asked for it (ASIC 22-084MR)

items.label: ASIC v Westpac, 2020
items.detail: Full Federal Court majority dismissed ASIC's responsible lending appeal (ASIC 20-149MR)

items.label: Telstra Super, 2026
items.detail: First ASIC case under the enforceable IDR requirements; liability found (ASIC 26-091MR)

cards.title: Match the timeframe to the duty
cards.prompt: Link each timeframe to the obligation it belongs to.

pairs.right: Unsuitability assessment made before the credit day (NCCP Act s 128)
Copy of the credit assessment, if requested within 2 years of the credit day
Review a TMD after a trigger; report significant dealings
IDR response to hardship notice and default notice complaints
IDR response to a standard complaint
Report a reportable situation to ASIC (s 912DAA)

cards.title: Final boss warm-up

cards.front: What is the core conduct standard in both licences?
cards.back: Do all things necessary to provide services efficiently, honestly and fairly.

cards.front: Two limbs of unsuitability?
cards.back: Likely unable to repay, or only with substantial hardship; or the credit does not meet requirements and objectives.

cards.front: What does DDO require of distributors?
cards.back: Do not distribute without a TMD; take reasonable steps for consistent distribution; report significant dealings and complaint numbers; keep records.

cards.front: When is a written IDR response still needed within five business days?
cards.back: When the customer asks, or for complaints about hardship, a declined insurance claim or its value, and certain trustee decisions.

cards.front: Is the Banking Code law?
cards.back: No. It is an ASIC-approved industry code that binds subscribing banks through their customer contracts and is monitored by the Banking Code Compliance Committee.

cards.front: Who receives unresolved complaints?
cards.back: AFCA, the external dispute resolution scheme every licensee providing services to retail clients must join.

cards.question: Product data shows complaints about a home loan feature tripled after a branch campaign. Who should hear about it under the bank's DDO arrangements?
options: Nobody, unless AFCA receives a complaint
Only the marketing team that ran the campaign
The product issuer team, because complaint information feeds TMD review
Only the branch manager
cards.explanation: TMDs specify the complaint and other information distributors must report to the issuer so it can decide whether the TMD needs review. A spike may be a review trigger.

cards.title: Real case: what the judges and ASIC emphasised
cards.body:
Across the cases in this quest, the official releases repeat a few lessons:

- **Systems and people together.** NAB's hardship failures came mostly from staff misusing a 'reject' button; Westpac's came from inadequate systems and operational failures.
- **Know your obligations.** In the Amex case, the Court noted that staff monitoring the TMDs were not aware of their obligations.
- **Penalties must sting.** The Amex judge said the penalty had to be more than a cost of doing business; in Westpac's hardship case the judge called a $10 million penalty 'derisory'.
- **Delay is harm.** Telstra Super's judge said timeliness is central to complaint management.

Training, supervision and monitoring are how a bank avoids becoming the next case.

cards.title: Quest take-aways
items: ASIC looks for one connected conduct system built on the licence general obligations.
Train, assess and record competence for each role before people serve customers, then refresh it.
Link complaints, lending file reviews and product data so signals reach the right team fast.
Escalate possible breaches promptly; reportable situations go to ASIC within 30 days.
Boards set accountabilities for complaints and systemic issues and receive complaint metrics.

cards.prompt: If you were the person ASIC interviewed about your role next week, which three records would you want to show, and are they complete today?

quiz.question: Under NCCP Act s 47(1)(k), what must a credit licensee have in addition to compliance arrangements and systems?
options: An external auditor's certificate each month
A written plan that documents those arrangements and systems
Approval of its training courses by AFCA
A board member responsible for each branch
quiz.explanation: Section 47(1)(k) requires adequate arrangements and systems to ensure compliance with s 47, and a written plan documenting them.

quiz.question: Which evidence best shows that a bank's complaints process meets RG 271?
options: A customer satisfaction survey average
The number of staff in the complaints team
A copy of the AFCA membership certificate alone
A complaints register showing receipt dates, responses within timeframes, delay notices and escalated systemic issues
quiz.explanation: RG 271 requires firms to record all complaints and manage timeframes and systemic issues. A register showing those elements is direct evidence; satisfaction scores and headcount are not.

quiz.question: A file review finds a lender approved loans without completing responsible lending training. What should happen first to protect customers?
options: Let her continue and complete training within the year
Review only the files that have generated complaints
Stop her approving loans until trained and assessed, and review all her files
Ask her to sign a statement that she understands the law
quiz.explanation: The bank must ensure representatives are trained and competent before they perform credit activities, and the whole population of files may carry the same gap. Complaints are not the only sign of harm.

quiz.question: According to RG 271, what must board or executive complaint reports include if the firm provides them?
options: Only the number of complaints sent to AFCA
Only complaints about senior staff
Metrics and analysis of complaints, including systemic issues identified
Only complaints resolved in the customer's favour
quiz.explanation: RG 271.119 says reports to the board or executive committees must include metrics and analysis of consumer complaints, including systemic issues found through them.

quiz.question: Which of these is the clearest link between complaints handling and the design and distribution obligations?
options: Distributors report complaint numbers to the issuer so it can decide whether a TMD needs review
AFCA approves each TMD after reviewing complaints
Complaints must be closed before a TMD can be made
Only the issuer may receive complaints about a product
quiz.explanation: TMDs set reporting periods for complaint numbers and other information distributors must give the issuer, which uses it to identify review needs.

quiz.question: What is the general purpose of the requirement to take reasonable steps so representatives comply with the law (s 912A(1)(ca) and s 47(1)(e))?
options: Representatives become solely liable for their own breaches
Representatives must hold their own separate licences
The licensee only answers for conduct at head office
The licensee stays responsible for supervising and monitoring its representatives' conduct
quiz.explanation: Both Acts require the licensee to take reasonable steps so its representatives comply. That is why supervision, monitoring and training records matter.

quiz.question: A pattern of complaints reveals a fee error affecting thousands of customers. What should the bank do once the issue is confirmed, according to RG 271?
options: Wait for each customer to complain individually
Promptly identify affected customers and provide fair remediation
Refund only customers who escalate to AFCA
Correct the system but not contact customers
quiz.explanation: RG 271 expects firms that confirm a systemic issue to take prompt action to identify affected consumers and provide fair remediation, alongside any reporting duties.

quiz.question: Which statement about the Banking Code of Practice is accurate for training purposes?
options: It is legislation enforced by ASIC through civil penalties
It is an ASIC-approved industry code that binds subscribing banks through their customer contracts
It applies only to small business lending
It replaces RG 271 for subscribing banks
quiz.explanation: ASIC's approval release says the Code binds ABA members as part of their customer contracts, that ASIC does not enforce it, and the Banking Code Compliance Committee monitors compliance. RG 271 still applies.

quiz.question: In the Amex DDO case, what did the Court note about staff responsible for monitoring the TMDs?
options: They had deliberately hidden the data
They were not aware of their obligations
They had reported the trigger to ASIC on time
They worked for David Jones, not Amex
quiz.explanation: ASIC's 24-158MR quotes the Court noting that those responsible for monitoring the TMDs were not aware of their obligations, while those aware of the facts did not act.

quiz.question: Which role is best placed to spot the first sign that a product is reaching customers outside its target market?
options: Frontline staff who hear customers' circumstances and escalate concerns
The external auditor at year end
AFCA case managers
The bank's share registry
quiz.explanation: Frontline representatives see mismatches first, which is why training on target markets and clear escalation routes are part of reasonable steps under DDO.

regulators: Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), external dispute resolution scheme

references.title: Corporations Act 2001
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: General obligations of AFS licensees, including trained and competent representatives (with CPD where it applies) and IDR plus AFCA membership for retail clients; reportable situations must be reported to ASIC within 30 days.

references.title: National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: General conduct obligations of credit licensees, including trained and competent representatives, IDR, AFCA membership and a written compliance plan; the resources and risk management limb does not apply to APRA-regulated bodies.

references.title: National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: Assessment within 90 days before the credit day; reasonable inquiries and verification; when a contract is unsuitable, including the home-sale presumption and the credit card limit test; free written assessment on request within 7 or 21 business days; ban on unsuitable contracts.

references.title: National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009, Schedule 1 (National Credit Code)
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: A debtor may give a hardship notice orally or in writing; the credit provider may request information within 21 days and must give a decision notice, with reasons and AFCA details if no change is agreed, within the set period.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 146 Licensing: Training of financial product advisers
references.note: Training standards for advisers; staff advising only on basic deposit and related non-cash payment products can meet them through a course assessed by their licensee; licensees need continuing training policies.

references.title: RG 206 Credit licensing: Competence and training
references.note: Credit licensees must keep representatives adequately trained and competent; ASIC expects initial and ongoing training built into recruitment and supervision.

references.title: RG 105 AFS licensing: Organisational competence
references.note: Guidance on the licensee's organisational competence; it notes the separate duty to keep representatives trained and competent.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 209 Credit licensing: Responsible lending conduct
references.note: ASIC's view of the inquiries, verification and unsuitability assessment required before credit is provided or increased, the limited role of benchmarks and the value of records.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 274 Product design and distribution obligations
references.provision: Tables 1-2; RG 274.20-274.21, 274.31, 274.154; RG 274.174 and Table 6 (distributor training and incentives)
references.note: TMD content, reasonable steps, reviews within 10 business days of a trigger, significant dealing notices within 10 business days and records; ASIC considers distributor staff training and incentives.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 271 Internal dispute resolution
references.note: Complaint definition, IDR response content and maximum timeframes (30 days standard, 21 days for hardship and default notice complaints), the five-business-day rule, systemic issues and staff training.

references.title: 24-136MR ASIC approves enhanced Banking Code of Practice
references.note: ASIC approved the 2025 Banking Code of Practice from 28 February 2025; the Code binds ABA members through their customer contracts, ASIC does not enforce it, and the Banking Code Compliance Committee oversees compliance.

references.title: Banking Code of Practice (2025)
references.note: Industry code binding on subscribing banks through their customer contracts. Its text was not opened for this quest, so no clause numbers are cited.

bank.question: Coral Range Bank offers deposit accounts, arranges consumer credit insurance with its cards and provides home loans. Which combination of licences does it typically need for these consumer services?
options: Only an Australian credit licence, because a bank's deposits are prudentially regulated
Only an AFS licence, because credit is a financial product under the Corporations Act
A banking authority from APRA, which replaces both ASIC licences
An AFS licence for the financial products and an Australian credit licence for the consumer credit
bank.explanation: Financial products such as deposits and insurance fall under the Corporations Act AFS licence, and consumer credit falls under the NCCP Act credit licence. APRA authorisation as an ADI does not replace ASIC licensing.

bank.question: A bank's contact centre staff handle calls about deposit accounts and payment products. The training team asks whether these staff fall under the representative training duty. What is the best answer?
options: No: the duty applies only to financial advisers giving personal advice on investments
Yes: s 912A(1)(f) covers representatives who provide the licensed financial services, including on basic deposit and payment products
No: deposit products are regulated by APRA, so ASIC training duties do not apply
Only if the staff are paid a commission on each product they sell
bank.explanation: Section 912A(1)(f) requires representatives to be adequately trained and competent to provide the financial services covered by the licence. RG 146 even addresses training for staff advising on basic deposit and non-cash payment products.

bank.question: Sofia is designing training for staff who give general advice only on basic deposit products. Under RG 146, which approach can meet the training standard?
options: Any internal course, without assessing it against the training standards
A course the bank itself has assessed as meeting the relevant knowledge and skill requirements
A course approved by AFCA's training panel
An external degree in any discipline
bank.explanation: RG 146 allows licensees to assess whether courses on basic deposit products and related non-cash payment products meet the training standards. The course must still be assessed against them; AFCA has no such role.

bank.question: Which statement about continuing training reflects RG 146?
options: Continuing training is optional once an adviser passes the initial course
Continuing training must be listed on a register and assessed every year
Continuing training only applies to advisers on Tier 1 products
Licensees must have policies so advisers keep their knowledge and skills up to date, and those courses need not be assessed by an authorised assessor
bank.explanation: RG 146.14-146.15 say licensees must implement policies and procedures for continuing training, and ASIC does not require continuing training courses to be assessed by an authorised assessor.

bank.question: A regional manager argues that because Coral Range Bank is APRA-regulated, the NCCP Act general obligations do not apply to its lenders. How accurate is that?
options: Correct: APRA regulation removes all credit licence obligations
Correct, but only for home loans secured by property
Wrong: APRA-regulated bodies have extra NCCP training duties instead
Mostly wrong: only the adequate resources and risk management limb is disapplied for APRA-regulated bodies
bank.explanation: Section 47(1)(l) applies unless the licensee is a body regulated by APRA. Every other s 47(1) duty, including training and competence, IDR and AFCA membership, still applies.

bank.question: In the 2022 Westpac consumer credit insurance case, which Corporations Act general obligation did Westpac admit failing?
options: Maintaining adequate financial resources under s 912A(1)(d)
Having a dispute resolution system under s 912A(1)(g)
Complying with licence conditions under s 912A(1)(b)
Complying with the financial services laws under s 912A(1)(c)
bank.explanation: ASIC's 22-084MR states Westpac admitted contravening s 12DM of the ASIC Act and failing to comply with financial services laws under s 912A(1)(c).

bank.question: Coral Range Bank learns on 3 March that there are reasonable grounds to believe a reportable situation has arisen. The compliance team wants to wait for the April board meeting before reporting. What is the risk?
options: The report is due to ASIC within 30 days of 3 March, so waiting for the board could make it late
None, because the deadline runs from the board's approval
None, because reports are only due once customers are remediated
The report must go to AFCA, not ASIC, so the timing does not matter
bank.explanation: Section 912DAA(3) sets 30 days from when the licensee first knows, or is reckless about, reasonable grounds to believe the situation has arisen. Board timing and remediation do not move the deadline.

bank.question: Which change at Coral Range Bank would most clearly require new or refreshed representative training to stay within s 47(1)(g)?
options: Moving the head office to a new building
Changing the bank's logo and branding colours
Launching a new credit product that lenders will arrange from next month
Appointing a new external auditor
bank.explanation: The duty is to keep representatives trained and competent for the credit activities they engage in. A new credit product changes those activities; the other changes do not.

bank.question: Why did the NAB hardship case (2025) illustrate a competence problem as well as a systems problem?
options: NAB staff were not licensed by ASIC to discuss hardship
NAB had no hardship policy at all
Staff misused a function in the hardship system, so customers who asked for help got no response
NAB staff gave customers personal financial advice
bank.explanation: ASIC explained that the failures mostly came from staff incorrectly using a 'reject' button. Competence includes knowing how the bank's systems carry out legal duties.

bank.question: A customer applies to increase her credit card limit through the app. Which responsible lending steps apply?
options: The same inquiry, verification and unsuitability assessment as for a new credit contract
None, because she is an existing customer with a good record
Only a credit report check, because the increase is small
Only the steps the card's TMD lists
bank.explanation: Sections 128-133 apply to increasing the credit limit of an existing contract as well as entering a new one. An existing relationship does not remove the steps.

bank.question: A lender tells a customer by email that she is 'approved, no conditions' for a car loan before doing any assessment. Why is this a responsible lending problem?
options: It is only a marketing issue, covered by the Banking Code
Section 128 also bars making an unconditional representation of eligibility without the assessment and inquiries
It breaches the design and distribution obligations but not the NCCP Act
It is acceptable if the loan is later declined
bank.explanation: Section 128(aa) prohibits making an unconditional representation that a consumer is eligible to enter a credit contract unless the assessment, inquiries and verification have been done within the required period.

bank.question: Liam's assessment of a couple was made 100 days before settlement because of a delayed property purchase. What should happen before the credit day?
options: Nothing, because the original approval remains valid until settlement
Only a new property valuation
A fresh assessment covering the credit day, with updated inquiries and verification
Only a signed declaration that nothing has changed
bank.explanation: Section 128 requires the assessment and inquiries to be made within 90 days before the credit day and to cover the period in which it falls. An assessment 100 days earlier does not meet that.

bank.question: A retired couple seek a 30-year loan they can only repay by selling their home in later years. They insist they are happy to do that. How should the lender approach unsuitability?
options: Approve, because the customers' wishes override the presumption
Start from the legal presumption of substantial hardship and only proceed if it is genuinely rebutted on the evidence
Approve, because the home secures the loan in any case
Decline automatically, because the presumption can never be rebutted
bank.explanation: Sections 131(3) and 133(3) presume substantial hardship where repayment depends on selling the principal residence, unless the contrary is proved. The presumption is strong but rebuttable; it cannot simply be waived by preference.

bank.question: A credit card applicant could manage the minimum repayments but could not repay the full proposed limit within the period ASIC determines. What follows under the NCCP Act?
options: She is taken to be able to comply only with substantial hardship, so the contract must be assessed as unsuitable
The card is suitable because minimum repayments are affordable
The card is suitable if she agrees to a lower annual fee
The lender may proceed if a guarantor signs
bank.explanation: Section 131(3AA) treats a credit card consumer as able to comply only with substantial hardship if they could not repay an amount equal to the limit within ASIC's period, which makes the contract unsuitable.

bank.question: Which use of an expense benchmark is consistent with RG 209?
options: Replacing the expense question on the application with the benchmark figure
Using the lowest benchmark figure so more applicants qualify
Comparing a first home buyer's estimated future expenses with a realistic benchmark to test plausibility
Using a benchmark from several years ago because it is simpler
bank.explanation: RG 209 says benchmarks can test plausibility, including estimating future outgoings, but they must be current and realistic, and they do not substitute for inquiries or verification.

bank.question: Under RG 209's idea of 'scalability', which application most justifies deeper inquiry and verification?
options: A small, short-term loan for a customer with clear, stable income
A large, long-term loan for a customer with irregular income and signs of financial stress
A loan to a customer who has banked with the lender for many years
A loan application submitted through the lender's app
bank.explanation: RG 209 explains that what is reasonable depends on the consumer's circumstances and the credit. Larger, longer credit plus risk signs call for more inquiry and verification.

bank.question: A customer asks in year five for a copy of the assessment for her personal loan and offers to pay a fee to speed it up. What is right?
options: Provide it within 7 business days and charge the fee
Decline, because the duty ends after two years
Provide it only if she lodges a complaint first
Provide a written copy within 21 business days, without charging
bank.explanation: Section 132(2) covers requests within 7 years; after 2 years the copy is due within 21 business days. Section 132(4) bans requesting or demanding payment for it.

bank.question: Which statement best describes the significance of ASIC's responsible lending case against Westpac (2019-2020)?
options: The courts found Westpac breached the law and ordered a record penalty
The High Court confirmed benchmarks must never be used
The case was settled with Westpac admitting all allegations
The courts rejected ASIC's case, and ASIC said it would review its guidance in light of the decision
bank.explanation: Justice Perram dismissed the case in 2019 and the Full Federal Court dismissed ASIC's appeal 2-1 in 2020. ASIC then said it would not appeal further and would review RG 209.

bank.question: Coral Range Bank issues a basic savings account and a 31-day term deposit. Do the design and distribution obligations apply?
options: No: deposit products are fully excluded from the DDO regime
Yes: basic banking products, including 31-day term deposits, are prescribed as needing a TMD
Only the term deposit, because savings accounts are not financial products
Only if the products are sold through a third-party distributor
bank.explanation: RG 274 notes that the regulations require a TMD for basic banking products, and that basic banking products include 31-day term deposits.

bank.question: Which item must a TMD contain under s 994B(5), as summarised in RG 274?
options: The names of the staff members who will sell the product
The kinds of information distributors must report, and how often, so the issuer can tell whether a review is needed
The product's expected profit margin
A credit assessment for each expected customer
bank.explanation: RG 274's summary of s 994B(5) includes reporting periods for complaint numbers and the other information distributors must report. Staff names, margins and individual assessments are not TMD content.

bank.question: A product owner wants to describe the target market of a new card as 'all adults in Australia'. Why is that unlikely to work?
options: TMDs can only describe consumers aged under 65
ASIC must approve the wording of every target market
The TMD must be appropriate: consumers reached under it must be likely to be in the target market and the product likely to fit their needs
A target market can only be described by postcode
bank.explanation: RG 274 explains the appropriateness requirement in s 994B(8). A market drawn so widely that the product is unlikely to suit many in it fails that test.

bank.question: Farid's team finds a review trigger occurred two weeks ago and nobody acted. What must the issuer do now?
options: Stop issuing the product, direct distributors to stop, and review the TMD before distribution resumes
Keep issuing until the next scheduled periodic review
Notify AFCA and continue distribution
Lower the product's fees and keep selling
bank.explanation: RG 274.154 says that if information reasonably suggests a TMD is no longer appropriate, the issuer must stop issuing and direct distributors to stop until it has reviewed the TMD (s 994C(3)-(5)).

bank.question: Which statement about 'significant dealings' is correct?
options: Issuers notify ASIC of significant dealings inconsistent with the TMD within 10 business days
Distributors notify ASIC directly within 30 days
Significant dealings are only reported once a year
Only dealings that cause a complaint are reportable
bank.explanation: Under s 994G an issuer that becomes aware of a significant dealing inconsistent with the TMD must notify ASIC as soon as practicable, within 10 business days. Distributors notify the issuer within the same limit.

bank.question: A distributor's staff are well trained on fees but cannot say who a home loan product is designed for. What does RG 274 suggest?
options: Nothing more is needed if fee disclosure is accurate
Replace the training with a longer product disclosure document
Train staff on key product attributes and the target market, and assess their skills
Ask customers to read the TMD and decide for themselves
bank.explanation: RG 274 says ASIC will consider whether distributors gave sufficient training and assessed staff skills, including on key product attributes and the target market, alongside sales conduct.

bank.question: A bonus scheme pays tellers for every credit card application, whether or not the customer fits the TMD. What is the best DDO response?
options: Keep the scheme but add a disclaimer to the application
Redesign or manage the incentive so it does not encourage distribution outside the target market
Keep the scheme because incentives are outside the DDO
Cancel all sales training to reduce pressure
bank.explanation: RG 274 says ASIC takes into account the steps a distributor takes to eliminate or manage the risk that incentives encourage harm or distribution inconsistent with the TMD.

bank.question: In ASIC's 2022 credit insurance release, what did ASIC say its earlier review of the sector had found?
options: Consumer credit insurance was poor value and sales practices and design caused consumer harm
Consumer credit insurance was good value but disclosure was unclear
Only one lender had sold policies poorly
The policies were sold mainly to small businesses
bank.explanation: ASIC's 22-084MR refers to Report 622, which found consumer credit insurance was poor value and that its sales practices and product design caused consumer harm across lenders.

bank.question: A customer tells a branch officer her loan statement is confusing and asks for an explanation. The officer explains it and she leaves satisfied. Is this a complaint?
options: Not unless she expressed dissatisfaction expecting a response; a simple request for information is usually an inquiry
Yes, every customer contact is a complaint under RG 271
Yes, because she visited a branch in person
No, because verbal contacts are never complaints
bank.explanation: RG 271's definition turns on an expression of dissatisfaction where a response or resolution is expected. Pure inquiries are not complaints, but verbal dissatisfaction can be.

bank.question: Kirra closes a complaint on day 4 with an apology because the customer was upset that the bank declined her loan application, which was a commercial decision. Does RG 271 require a written IDR response?
options: Yes, all declined loan complaints need a written response
Yes, because any apology must be in writing
Not unless she asks for one, because an explanation or apology can close it within five business days
No, and she also loses the right to go to AFCA
bank.explanation: RG 271.71 and 271.74 allow closure within five business days with an explanation or apology, giving refusal of credit as an example. A written response is still needed if she requests it. Her AFCA rights are unaffected.

bank.question: A credit complaint involves a default notice the bank sent. What is the maximum IDR response timeframe under RG 271?
options: 30 calendar days after receiving the complaint
45 calendar days after receiving the complaint
21 calendar days after receiving the complaint
5 business days after receiving the complaint
bank.explanation: RG 271's Table 2 sets 21 calendar days for credit-related complaints involving default notices, and for those involving hardship notices or requests to postpone enforcement.

bank.question: Coral Range Bank rejects a complaint about fees. Which content must the IDR response include to meet RG 271.54?
options: Only the decision and a phone number for the branch
A copy of the bank's full complaints policy
A statement that the decision is final and cannot be reviewed
The issues raised, findings on material facts with supporting information, and enough detail for an informed decision about AFCA
bank.explanation: RG 271.54 requires the reasons to identify and address the issues, set out findings on material questions of fact with supporting information, and give enough detail for the complainant to decide whether to go to AFCA.

bank.question: Which statement about AFCA membership is accurate?
options: Only banks with more than one million customers must join AFCA
AFS licensees serving retail clients and credit licensees must be members of the AFCA scheme
AFCA membership is voluntary for credit licensees
AFCA membership replaces the need for an IDR process
bank.explanation: Section 912A(1)(g) and (2) require AFS licensees serving retail clients to have IDR and AFCA membership, and s 47(1)(h)-(i) require credit licensees to have IDR and be AFCA members. Membership does not replace IDR.

bank.question: After receiving a hardship notice, what may a credit provider do under National Credit Code s 72(2) if it needs more information?
options: Within 21 days, ask the debtor for specified relevant information to be provided within 21 days
Refuse to consider the notice until the debtor attends a branch
Wait 90 days before deciding
Charge a fee to assess the notice
bank.explanation: Section 72(2) lets the credit provider, within 21 days of receiving the hardship notice, require specified information relevant to the decision, to be given within 21 days.

bank.question: A customer whose first language is not English struggles to explain her complaint on the phone. What does RG 271 expect?
options: Ask her to put the complaint in writing in English
Close the complaint because it cannot be understood
Refer her straight to AFCA
An accessible process, such as interpreter or translation help, and staff trained to identify and support her
bank.explanation: RG 271 requires an IDR process that people with language difficulties can use, suggests translation services, and expects staff to be trained to identify and help people who need assistance to complain.

bank.question: Which statement best reflects how the Banking Code of Practice should be described in staff training?
options: An ASIC-approved industry code that subscribing banks follow under their customer contracts, monitored by the Banking Code Compliance Committee
A regulation made by ASIC under the Corporations Act and enforced by civil penalty
An APRA prudential standard on customer service
A voluntary guide with no effect on customer contracts
bank.explanation: ASIC's 24-136MR explains the Code binds ABA members and forms part of contracts with customers, ASIC does not enforce it, and the BCCC monitors compliance and can apply sanctions.

bank.question: ASIC asks Coral Range Bank how it knows its credit representatives are competent. Which response is strongest?
options: Role-based training plans, dated completion and assessment records, supervision results and refresher logs
A statement that all staff signed the code of conduct
The number of training hours delivered across the bank
Customer satisfaction scores for the lending team
bank.explanation: Competence is shown by evidence for each role and person: what training was required, what was completed and assessed, and how supervision confirmed it. Aggregate hours and satisfaction scores do not show individual competence.

bank.question: A mock file review finds a lender relied only on benchmarks for living expenses in several files. What is the most complete response?
options: Correct the two sampled files and close the review
Issue a reminder email to all lenders
Review her other files, remediate any unsuitable lending, retrain and supervise her, and refer for breach assessment
Wait for complaints before acting
bank.explanation: The finding points to a competence gap and possibly a breach. Reviewing the full population, remediating, retraining and breach assessment address the cause and the harm.

bank.question: Which link between teams best supports the DDO review obligation?
options: Marketing sharing campaign artwork with branches
Finance sharing quarterly profit forecasts with branches
HR sharing leave rosters with the complaints team
Complaints data flowing promptly from distributors to the product issuer team
bank.explanation: TMDs specify complaint and other information distributors report to the issuer so it can identify when a TMD may no longer be appropriate.

bank.question: A complaints analyst spots dozens of complaints about the same interest calculation error. Put simply, what does RG 271 require next?
options: Promptly escalate the possible systemic issue for investigation, then report internally on the outcome
Answer each complaint separately and take no further action
Wait until the next annual complaints report
Forward all the complaints to AFCA
bank.explanation: RG 271.120 requires firms to escalate possible systemic issues promptly to the right area for investigation and to report internally on outcomes. RG 271.117 lists interest calculation errors as an example.

bank.question: Who must set clear accountabilities for complaints handling, including systemic issues, under RG 271?
options: AFCA
The Banking Code Compliance Committee
The board (or owners of smaller firms)
Each individual complaints officer
bank.explanation: RG 271.118 says boards must set clear accountabilities for complaints handling functions, including management of systemic issues identified through complaints.

bank.question: Which pairing of obligation and timeframe is correct?
options: Respond to a standard bank complaint: within 45 calendar days
Review a TMD after a review trigger: within 10 business days
Report a reportable situation to ASIC: within 90 days
Make the unsuitability assessment: within 30 days before the credit day
bank.explanation: TMD reviews after a trigger are due within 10 business days. Standard complaints have 30 calendar days, reportable situations 30 days, and the unsuitability assessment must be within 90 days before the credit day.

bank.question: A regional manager suggests delaying a hardship decision for a customer so the bank 'has time to get the paperwork right'. Which combination of cases shows the risk?
options: American Express (2024) and Westpac (2022), both about credit insurance
ASIC v Westpac (2020) and Telstra Super (2026), both about lending
Telstra Super (2026) and American Express (2024), both about DDO
Westpac (2026) and NAB with AFSH (2025), both penalised for hardship responses not given in time
bank.explanation: The Westpac and NAB/AFSH hardship cases led to penalties of $26 million and $15.5 million for failing to respond to hardship notices within the legal time. The other pairings misdescribe the cases.
